marks.c1-why: codex: Fiscal 2027 revenue is central to NVIDIA’s earnings outlook and valuation, with consensus around $406–412 billion. Data center accounted for roughly 92% of second-quarter revenue, making its annual performance a major matter to track. | claude: Fiscal 2027 revenue, and data-center revenue at about 92% of it, is NVIDIA's central fundamental bet, so it directly sets revenue, profit and valuation. That week's articles carry live data that would move such an answer: Q2 data-center revenue of $89.0B (+117%), Q3 guidance of $108B ±2%, and consensus diverging between $406B and $412B. The library should hold one question here, folding the quarterly checkpoints into it as milestones of the same bet.
marks.c2-why: codex: An investment of up to $10 billion is large enough to matter to Nvidia’s cash deployment and investment exposure, even relative to its substantial profit. The reported talks make an agreement plausible, but neither the amount nor the time remaining establishes that agreement is more likely than not; the unconfirmed IPO timing and Huang’s earlier remark add uncertainty. | claude: Worth (kept no): the other analyst's case rests on cash deployment, but the article puts the possible stake at up to $10B, about a sixth of one quarter's $59.7B profit and roughly 0.5% of Anthropic, bought on the same terms as other IPO buyers and with no hardware commitment attached. At that scale it cannot change Nvidia's revenue, profit, cash or credit risk. The portfolio-exposure concern ($99B of equity investments) is a broader matter that this one bet does not decide. Supported (kept yes): Reuters reports talks for this specific anchor role at a specific amount, and Nvidia has taken an IPO cornerstone role before (Arm, 2023). Even if the listing slips past the November 2026 midterms, about ten months remain before the deadline. Huang's 'probably the last' remark was tied to companies going public, which argues against further private rounds rather than against an IPO anchor role. The non-confirmation, the single unnamed source and the risk that the IPO slips past the deadline lower confidence but do not justify No over Yes.
marks.c3-why: codex: The scale of NVIDIA’s credit support and guarantees could materially affect its credit risk. The present answer is below $10 billion, but the cited reporting describes up to $105 billion in disclosed maximum guarantee exposure and the reasons themselves support the $100 billion-or-more choice. | claude: Guarantee and credit-support exposure reported above $100 billion (up to $105 billion maximum, tied to OpenAI/SB Energy lease obligations) is a material credit-risk bet worth tracking. The present answer is rung 1 (below $10 billion), but its own reasons and the cited statements e42 and e61 argue for rung 5 ($100 billion or more), so the evidence contradicts the answer shown.
marks.c4-why: codex: The reported purchase and supply plans imply a potentially material China opportunity, and MIIT's reported intent to approve purchases supports Yes as the most likely outcome despite timing and policy uncertainty. The earlier restriction on a related workstation GPU adds countervailing precedent without changing the answer; the revenue guidance describes financial context rather than the likelihood of MIIT approval. | claude: This is worth tracking: a reported ~1M-unit ByteDance order at over $6,000 per card means billions in China revenue that guidance currently excludes. Rung 1 is supported because several outlets, all relaying The Information, say MIIT told specific firms it intends to approve RTX Pro 5500 purchases, with four months left before the deadline; the reasons weigh the H200 and domestic-chip precedents against that. The 2025 RTX Pro 6000D stop-buying order is another Beijing-reversal precedent that only tempers confidence, while the Q3 guidance carve-out says nothing about whether MIIT will approve.
marks.c5-why: codex: Customer financing and guarantees are large enough to affect NVIDIA’s cash and credit risk, so the question is worth tracking. I keep supported as no: the disclosed guarantee ceilings do not establish what will be outstanding or included in the next commitments note, and the other amounts shown do not bridge that gap; the $25 billion of committed equity investments is not shown to fall entirely within the question’s category. | claude: Worth (agreed): guarantees and credit support of $105–108.5 billion tied to OpenAI leases and neoclouds can materially change NVIDIA's cash and credit risk. Supported (kept yes): NVIDIA has already disclosed a $105 billion maximum guarantee exposure, and src-5 describes $108.5 billion guarantee obligations as a capped balance-sheet exposure. Commitments notes customarily report guarantees at their maximum potential amount, so the next note falling below $25 billion would need that disclosed exposure to shrink by more than three-quarters, and nothing shown suggests that. The other analyst is right that the $25 billion of committed equity investments may sit outside this category, but rung 5 does not depend on it; the ceilings alone clear the $25 billion threshold, and the Nscale $1 billion commitment and $860.3 million guarantee only add to it.
marks.c6-why: codex: The roughly $13 billion acquisition is large and strategically significant enough to track. The reported agreement and later descriptions of Hugging Face as acquired support completion as the most likely outcome by March 2028, although the pending report and absence of a cited filing or completion announcement limit confidence that it has already closed. | claude: A roughly $13 billion cash acquisition, NVIDIA's second-largest ever and a deal that faces possible antitrust review, is large enough to matter for cash and strategy, so it is worth a card. With the deal announced on 3 September 2026, about 18 months before the deadline, and no report of repricing, termination or regulatory blockage, rung 1 is the right choice. The reasons correctly treat the loose 'has acquired' wording as weak and the Fool.com 'pending' note as a counterweight that does not move the answer to another rung.
marks.c7-why: codex: The potential order volumes and card prices imply a sales opportunity large enough to matter for Nvidia. The reported intention to approve purchases and Nvidia's shipment target support a forecast of permission by the deadline, although the reports are unconfirmed and do not establish that permission has already been granted. | claude: Chinese permission matters at Nvidia's scale: ByteDance's reported order of about 1 million cards at over $6,000 each, against planned China supply of 500,000 a quarter, is billions of dollars of revenue on top of guidance that assumes no China sales. The Yes answer rests on the reported MIIT statement that the government intends to approve purchases plus its request for quantities, which reasonably makes approval within four months more likely than not. The reasons correctly treat these as unconfirmed and count the repeated coverage as one report, though they skip the article's caution about Beijing's past reversals (RTX Pro 6000D, H200).
marks.c8-why: codex: Commitments of this scale can materially affect NVIDIA’s cash and inventory risk, and the reported $279 billion Q2 figure, together with sustained supply constraints, supports a year-end estimate above $200 billion. Huang’s chip-volume forecast reinforces that view; the inquiry into potential China purchases does not establish orders or a change in NVIDIA’s commitments. | claude: Supply commitments of $279bn against roughly $400bn of annual revenue are a material cash and credit exposure, so the question is worth holding. Three outlets report the Q2 figure of $279bn, up from $119bn, and management expects supply to stay constrained through FY2028; that makes a year-end figure of $200bn or more well supported, and the answer rightly does not add the vague $500bn HBM claim. Huang's pledge to double chip units in 2027 only reinforces rung 5, and the China MIIT inquiry does not bear on commitments.
marks.c9-why: codex: Blackwell access to China could materially affect Nvidia’s revenue. I keep supported as no: the answer treats the RTX Pro 5500 opportunity as unsized and narrows the question to data-center accelerators, although a cited article reports a potential million-unit AI order and planned shipments from late December; those details materially challenge its forecast of Still open, even though approval remains uncertain. Fact 1 adds uncertainty about U.S. clearance, while Fact 2 concerns unrelated agent-safety software. | claude: Supported (disputed): I keep yes. The answer does wrongly call the RTX Pro 5500 path 'unsized': cited article src-25 reports ByteDance weighing about 1 million units and Nvidia aiming to ship about 500k a quarter from late December. But those figures come from the same unverified Information report. Rung 1 also needs an actual U.S. authorization, and src-25 itself says Washington has not said whether the card may ship and that its exemption is only executives' reading. Blackwell accelerators remain barred, and China still curbs even the H200. So the slip raises rung 1's odds without displacing Still open, and nothing supports a post-September-23 formal prohibition for rung 2. Worth, Fact 1 and Fact 2 are undisputed and kept: Blackwell access to China is a multi-billion-dollar revenue bet that guidance excludes; Fact 1 only adds U.S.-side uncertainty; Fact 2 is unrelated agent-safety software.
marks.c10-why: codex: The hyperscalers’ combined data-center spending is a major driver of demand for NVIDIA’s products. The cited forecast of nearly $800 billion supports the present range, while the other evidence does not establish a comparable 2026 total in a different range. | claude: Combined big-five hyperscaler data-center capex is the main driver of NVIDIA's Data Center revenue, so it is a bet worth holding a card for. NVIDIA's own call guidance (e162, e367) says 'approach/nearly $800 billion' for 2026, and the reasons correctly treat Alphabet's $200 billion as a component, the ~$750 billion global AI-infrastructure figure as a different scope, and the $1.3 trillion as 2027, which justifies rung 3 over its neighbours. 'Nearly' leaves some risk of landing just under $775 billion, but nothing shown points there.
marks.c11-why: codex: The scale of NVIDIA’s customer financing and guarantees makes its cash and credit exposure worth tracking. The disclosed guarantee caps support the possibility of a total above $25 billion, but the material does not establish how much will remain outstanding or be included in the next commitments note; the smaller Nscale amounts and preliminary insurance talks do not resolve that gap. | claude: Worth (agreed): NVIDIA's guarantees, credit support and customer financing (a $105B to $108.5B guarantee cap, 4.25 GW plus a 3.75 GW option at PORTS-Pike, about 2 GW for another lab, Nscale) are large enough to move cash and credit risk. Supported (kept yes against the second reading): the $105B and $108.5B figures are maximum-exposure amounts NVIDIA itself disclosed (src-52, src-5), and a guarantee disclosure in a commitments note normally reports exactly that maximum potential payment, not the amount drawn. Even a figure well below the cap, such as a quarter of it, clears $25B, and nothing in the material points below that line. So rung 5 is justified over rung 4, while the reasons correctly treat the caps as ceilings and the insurer talks as early-stage.
marks.c12-why: codex: Vera Rubin’s ramp is material to NVIDIA’s revenue. Management’s reported expectation that it will contribute about 20% of fiscal Q3 data center revenue, together with production shipments already underway, supports forecasting Yes, although the required disclosure and revenue recognition have not yet been established. | claude: The Vera Rubin ramp is a revenue-scale bet for NVIDIA. Rung 1 is directly backed by NVIDIA's own statements: production shipments began in August with purchase orders from every major hyperscaler, and management expects Rubin to be about 20% of fiscal Q3 2027 Data Center revenue, recognised well before 31 January 2027. One cited item is miscast: e279's Micron article (fiscal 2025 figures, an October 2025 dividend) is a stale 2025 piece about Micron, not NVIDIA's Rubin revenue timing. It is used only to temper the confidence, though, and does not weaken the choice of rung 1.
marks.c13-why: codex: A roughly $13 billion acquisition is large enough to merit tracking. The announced agreement and reports describing the deal as completed support forecasting closure by March 2028, although the pending report and lack of a cited completion announcement limit confidence. | claude: A roughly $13 billion purchase, NVIDIA's second-largest ever, is a material cash outlay. Its close is a real antitrust bet given that competition regulators are already questioning NVIDIA's practices, so it is worth a card. 'Yes' is justified over its neighbours: the deal was announced on 3 September with about 18 months left to close, and nothing reports repricing, a regulatory challenge or termination. The reasons rightly treat the loose 'has since acquired' wording (ABC, Fox, Yahoo) as weaker than Wired's 'agreed' and Fool's 'pending', and so do not count it as proof of closing.
marks.c14-why: codex: I keep worth as yes: a roughly $13 billion acquisition is large enough to affect NVIDIA’s cash and merits tracking, even though the commitments-note wording is an indirect way to track it. I keep supported as no: the articles establish an agreed deal price, but do not establish what amount, if any, NVIDIA will report as a purchase commitment at fiscal year-end or justify the $10 billion–$15 billion range over a lower one. | claude: Worth (kept no): the other analyst is right that the deal is large in absolute terms, but at about $13B against roughly $97B of annual free cash flow it does not materially change NVIDIA's revenue, profit, cash or credit risk. The question also tracks a commitments-note figure rather than the deal itself; that figure turns on closing timing and on whether NVIDIA lists the acquisition there at all, so it is an accounting wording of the deal rather than a bet worth its own card. Supported (no, both agree): the reasons treat the announced price as the year-end commitment without addressing closing. A close before fiscal year-end would leave about zero, which is rung 1, and none of the cited statements or articles gives a closing date or regulatory timeline, so rung 3 is not justified over rung 1.
marks.c15-why: codex: Gross margin is material to NVIDIA’s profits, with each percentage point worth about $3 billion at the cited sales level. Management’s 72%–73% FY2028 outlook supports the neutral midpoint forecast; the industry-wide margin warning is unquantified and does not justify moving to a neighboring rung. | claude: FY2028 gross margin is a major bet for NVIDIA: each point is worth about $3 billion on trailing sales, and roughly $7 billion on the ~$700 billion FY2028 revenue implied by guidance. Several articles (e158, e200, e317) relay the CFO's guide of 72%–73% for FY2028, after a 71%–72% Q4 FY2027 bottom and with Q1 FY2028 price increases. Its 72.5% midpoint sits inside rung 3, and none of the cited evidence quantifies a move past the 73% or 71% boundaries, so the Neutral answer is justified over its neighbours.
marks.c16-why: codex: Hyperscaler data-center spending is a major driver of demand for NVIDIA’s products. The cited forecast of nearly $800 billion supports the present range, although its imprecision and reliance on reported estimates limit confidence. | claude: The big five hyperscalers' combined 2026 data-center capex is the main driver of NVIDIA's data-center revenue, so it is clearly worth tracking. The present answer, rung 3, rests on NVIDIA's own earnings-call figure of capex that will 'approach' or reach 'nearly' $800 billion (e162, e367), repeated by several outlets (e103, e119, e324). The reasons correctly treat Alphabet's $200 billion as part of that total, set aside the ~$750 billion global figure (e305) as a different scope, and set aside the $1.3 trillion figures (e469) as 2027. 'Nearly $800 billion' sits inside the $775–825 billion band, though close to the rung-2 boundary.
marks.c17-why: codex: NVIDIA's $279 billion in supply and capacity commitments is material to its ability to meet data center demand and creates substantial exposure if demand slows or products transition faster than expected. The size and trajectory of those commitments are worth tracking because they can affect revenue, costs and cash obligations. | claude: Supply and capacity commitments of $279B, up from $119B in one quarter, are about two-thirds of FY2027 consensus revenue. They are hard to reduce if demand slows, so they directly determine NVIDIA's cash, inventory write-down and margin risk, and an analyst would hold a card on them. The Fool piece's claim of a $500B HBM lock-in suggests the commitments may still be rising, which reinforces that the library should track this.
marks.c18-why: codex: FY2028 revenue growth is central to NVIDIA’s financial outlook. I keep supported as yes: management’s direct outlook of approximately 70% reasonably supports a bullish point estimate over the 65.5%–66% consensus, although the rounded guidance lies on the boundary and makes the choice uncertain. | claude: Worth (agreed, kept yes): FY2028 total revenue growth is a core, revenue-defining bet for NVIDIA. Supported (changed from no to yes): management's 'approximately 70%' guide is the strongest input and lands on rung 2's inclusive lower edge. The cited statements tilt it at or above 70%, not below: customer forecasts imply doubling (e46), the CEO says demand would be 'a lot higher' (e64), and an analyst expects sandbagging (e269). Consensus at 65.5–66% (e59, e368) lags a guide that itself jumped from the prior 45% model. So the reasons' tie-break is thin, but the cited material justifies rung 2 over rung 3.
marks.c19-why: codex: Data-center revenue is central to Nvidia’s financial performance. The cited $89 billion quarter does not justify the present answer of at least $450 billion, and the reasons instead select the $350–<$400 billion band. | claude: FY2027 data-center revenue is Nvidia's core bet (about 92.5% of sales), so the question is worth tracking. The present answer is marked as the ≥$450B rung, but the reasons explicitly forecast the $350–<$400B band, and the single cited fact ($89B in the latest quarter, about $356B annualized) does not justify ≥$450B over its neighbours.
